# Potaliya Sutta (MN 54 (PTS MN i 359))

**ID:** MN 54 (PTS MN i 359)
**Section:** Majjhimanikāya (mn)
**Collection:** Suttas-Early-1
**Title (Pali):** Potaliya Sutta
**PTS:** MN i 359
**tipitaka.org (CST):** https://tipitaka.org/romn/cscd/s0202m.mul0.xml

## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and catalog data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The *Potaliya Sutta* (MN 54, PTS MN i 359) is the 54th discourse of the Majjhimanikāya [Ñāṇamoli & Bodhi 1995]. Set in the town of Āpaṇa in the country of the Aṅguttarāpans, the dialogue begins when the householder Potaliya, strolling in a grove in full dress with parasol and sandals, takes offense at the Buddha addressing him as "householder" (*gahapati*), claiming that he has abandoned all worldly business [Ñāṇamoli & Bodhi 1995]. In response, the Buddha explains what the "cutting off of affairs" (*vohārasamuccheda*) actually means in the discipline of the Noble One [Humphreys 1956; Ñāṇamoli & Bodhi 1995; Rogell 2003]. He presents eight abandonments and illustrates the grave perils of sensual pleasures through an extended sequence of graphic similes: a hungry dog gnawing a meatless bone, a bird attacked by other birds for a piece of meat, a man carrying a burning grass torch against the wind, a deep charcoal pit into which one is dragged by two strong men, a dream of lovely parks that vanishes upon waking, borrowed finery that must be returned to its owners in the street, and a man climbing a tree for fruit while another cuts it down [Anālayo 2010; Anālayo 2014; Rogell 2003].
